title: Measurement protocol for non-adiabatic geometric phases of Floquet states
authors: Carlos Martín-Fernández, Gloria Platero, Sigmund Kohler
abstract: Periodically time-dependent quantum systems have Floquet solutions. They consist of a phase factor and a Floquet mode which shares the periodicity of the driving. Consequently, any such solution possesses a non adiabatic geometric phase known as the Aharonov-Anandan (AA) phase. It is gauge-invariant and, therefore, is experimentally accessible. We propose a protocol for the measurement of AA phases based on the adiabatic change of the phase of the non-adiabatic driving. We argue that the experimental requirements of the protocol are those of previous measurements of adiabatic phases.
summary: This paper details a novel measurement protocol to experimentally detect the Aharonov-Anandan geometric phase in quantum systems driven periodically (Floquet systems). By adapting spin-echo techniques and utilizing Ramsey interferometry, the authors show how to isolate this non-adiabatic phase from the dominant dynamical phase. This provides a powerful tool for characterizing geometric properties in driven quantum matter.
main_problem: The paper proposes a concrete measurement protocol for the Aharonov-Anandan (AA) geometric phase associated with Floquet states in periodically driven quantum systems.
main_result: The protocol successfully links the non-adiabatic AA phase to the adiabatic Floquet-Berry phase, allowing for measurement by adapting spin-echo techniques to cancel dynamical phases.
method: The measurement relies on adiabatically ramping the driving parameters and employing a sequence involving $\sigma_y$-pulses (similar to spin-echo) to isolate and measure the accumulated geometric phase via Ramsey interferometry.
model_or_system: The analysis uses a general periodically time-dependent Hamiltonian, illustrated by a driven two-level system (TLS) Hamiltonian, which models the quantum dynamics under periodic driving.
key_observables: The primary observable is the excitation probability ($P_e$) measured via Ramsey interferometry, which is related to the accumulated phase as $\cos^2(2\gamma_{AA})$.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the driving frequency ($\Omega$), the detuning ($\epsilon$), and the time scale of the measurement loop ($T_{	ext{loop}}$).
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes the ability to perform adiabatic following during parameter changes and requires applying $\pi$-pulses at multiples of the driving period ($t=kT$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Floquet spectrum, the step-by-step measurement protocol (preparation, phase tuning, $\sigma_y$-pulse), and simulations showing fidelity and excitation probability dependence on detuning and loop time.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the AA phase in Floquet systems, develops the measurement protocol by adapting spin-echo techniques, and then analyzes the protocol's feasibility and sensitivity to noise.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed, experimentally relevant blueprint for measuring non-adiabatic geometric phases in driven quantum systems, bridging the gap between theoretical Floquet theory and measurable quantum optics experiments.

FIG. 3. Simulation of the protocol sketched in Fig. 2 with prepara- tion in the ground state for tunneling ∆= Ω/2 and various detunings. (a) Phase of the overlap Z (thin lines) compared to the theoretically expected value 2γFB [broad matte line of same color, cf. Fig. 1(a)] for protocol time Tloop = 25T. The detunings are ε = 0 (red) and 0.3Ω(blue). (b,c) Loop fidelity |Z| for detunings ε = 0.0125Ω(b) and 0.3Ω(c) for various protocol times Tloop = NloopT. The vertical dotted lines mark positions of the quasienergy crossings in the ab- sence of detuning.

FIG. 2. Protocol for the cancellation of the dynamical phase. After preparation of the qubit in the ground state, the amplitude is ramped up with driving phase θ = 0. After time tramp, the amplitude is kept constant, while the drive phase θ is adiabatically increased during N driving periods until it reaches the value 2π. Next, a σy-pulse is applied, and the parameters are tuned back in the same way. A fi- nal σy-pulse restores the ground state. For Ramsey interference, a σy-pulse is applied initially to create a superposition between ground and excited state. Finally, the populations are measured by tomogra- phy.
